raw:
{
  "question_intent": "Inquire about Tesco restructuring costs and the impact of US election and US business activity on UK bank's budget and business activity.",
  "main_topics": ["Tesco restructuring costs", "UK bank's budget and business activity", "US election impact", "US business activity impact"],
  "answer_completeness": "Complete",
  "response_stance": "Direct",
  "evidence_level": "High",
  "contains_numeric_evidence": true,
  "contains_forward_guidance": true,
  "narrative_alignment": "Aligned",
  "question_quote": "If we think about the £30m a month, £350m or £360m year, let's say, should we be assuming that at some point we'll hear from you about £100m plus restructuring charge next year? Is that something to be aware of with Q4 results perhaps?",
  "answer_quote": "Thank you, Chris. On the Tesco point, I think your assessment of what you should build in as ongoing operational costs is accurate. I'm not going to comment at this point in terms of restructuring, we've actually been taking some costs as we've gone through the year in order to start that integration process for Tesco, so taking some into the run rate already. Clearly there will be more as we go forward. Our objective in the short term is to ensure that we integrate it safely and properly, and ensure customer service is unaffected. We'll just advise you as we go through 2025 really on the quantum and the timing of those integration costs. But our objective is for this business to be RoTE accretive, so you can imagine we do have some ambition around that [audio unclear]. For the target cost: income ratio for 2026, we are sticking to what we gave on the 20th February. Yes, the BUK cost: income ratio remains the same for 2026. On the budget point, we believe now is the right time to grow in the UK and we made that decision actually more than a year ago when we put our plan together that we presented that we presented in February. There is no part of the budget that would change our perspective on that. We believe that it aligns closely to the objectives of the government, which are really to drive growth in the UK. Clearly there will be some impacts on the cost base, but equally we're encouraged by that focus on investment and growth in the UK. That's probably where I'd leave that. In terms of the US, it's very early. Obviously, we need to see the expectations of that new administration. The things that we are mindful of really are the expectations of growth in the US and we saw some reflection of that in the immediate share price response both for us and U.S. banks. I think the second thing I would say is that we're really mindful of under waiting, is there the timing and nature of Basel 3.1 in in the US, they're the two things that we're watching for.",
  "reason": "The answer directly addresses the Tesco restructuring costs, the bank's budget and business activity, and the impact of the US election and business activity, providing specific details and forward guidance."
}

data.question_intent: Inquire about Tesco restructuring costs and the impact of US election and US business activity on UK bank's budget and business activity.
main_topics: UK bank's budget and business activity
data.question_quote: If we think about the £30m a month, £350m or £360m year, let's say, should we be assuming that at some point we'll hear from you about £100m plus restructuring charge next year? Is that something to be aware of with Q4 results perhaps?
data.answer_quote: Thank you, Chris. On the Tesco point, I think your assessment of what you should build in as ongoing operational costs is accurate. I'm not going to comment at this point in terms of restructuring, we've actually been taking some costs as we've gone through the year in order to start that integration process for Tesco, so taking some into the run rate already. Clearly there will be more as we go forward. Our objective in the short term is to ensure that we integrate it safely and properly, and ensure customer service is unaffected. We'll just advise you as we go through 2025 really on the quantum and the timing of those integration costs. But our objective is for this business to be RoTE accretive, so you can imagine we do have some ambition around that [audio unclear]. For the target cost: income ratio for 2026, we are sticking to what we gave on the 20th February. Yes, the BUK cost: income ratio remains the same for 2026. On the budget point, we believe now is the right time to grow in the UK and we made that decision actually more than a year ago when we put our plan together that we presented that we presented in February. There is no part of the budget that would change our perspective on that. We believe that it aligns closely to the objectives of the government, which are really to drive growth in the UK. Clearly there will be some impacts on the cost base, but equally we're encouraged by that focus on investment and growth in the UK. That's probably where I'd leave that. In terms of the US, it's very early. Obviously, we need to see the expectations of that new administration. The things that we are mindful of really are the expectations of growth in the US and we saw some reflection of that in the immediate share price response both for us and U.S. banks. I think the second thing I would say is that we're really mindful of under waiting, is there the timing and nature of Basel 3.1 in in the US, they're the two things that we're watching for.
data.reason: The answer directly addresses the Tesco restructuring costs, the bank's budget and business activity, and the impact of the US election and business activity, providing specific details and forward guidance.
